subtitle: Spot a shortcut in judgment, use the same criteria and a second reader, ask the question the task needs and check the results over time.
scope: All people and situations in this course are invented practice cases. No test, score or personal assessment is used. Real decisions keep their own criteria, reporting duties and equity analysis steps. Native American and Tribal-specific matters go to DHS Tribal and Urban Indian Relations and the person or area responsible.
introTranscript: A quick assumption can arrive before you know anything about the person in front of you. In this course, you follow a DHS team through a page review and a project assignment. You notice an assumption about age and technology, set criteria before reviewing anyone’s work, ask everyone the same task question and learn what different response styles mean. You also see when a concern becomes a civil rights duty, and how to check results over time. All cases are practice. No test, score or personal disclosure is required.

lessons.title: Notice a shortcut in judgment before it becomes a decision
lessons.summary: A quick connection can feel true before you know anything about the person. Notice it, and look at the decision it could change.
lessons.objective: Tell a quick assumption apart from information about the person and the task.
objectives: Tell a quick assumption apart from information about the person and the task.
Identify the age-to-technology assumption in the practice case.
Choose a next step that checks the assumption against the task.
takeaways: Feeling familiar is not the same as evidence.
Noticing an assumption is a skill, not a confession.
A helpful intention still deserves a check against the facts.
lessons.statement: Notice what came to mind, then ask what the facts about this person and this task actually show.

image.caption: Four people stand together in a hallway holding documents and a laptop.

intro.heading: What does Sana’s first impression tell her?
intro.body:
Sana and Emmett work on a DHS team that is testing a draft information page. Two colleagues, Dev and Quinn, have offered to walk the team through the page’s next step. Dev is older than Quinn. That is all Sana knows about their ages. She knows nothing yet about how either of them uses the page.

Before she asks anyone a question, Sana thinks that Quinn will probably handle the page better. The thought arrives fast and feels familiar. It is a shortcut in judgment: a link between youth and comfort with technology that she has heard many times. Feeling familiar does not make it true about Dev or Quinn.

Research on decision-making shows that quick links like this can shape choices, even when a person would reject the belief on reflection. Researchers often use the term “implicit bias” for this. In plain words, it means an assumption that acts before you have checked it. This course does not test or score anyone. It teaches the checks that keep an assumption from becoming a decision.

The thought matters because of what Sana plans next. She wants Quinn to go first, and she plans to offer Dev basic help. No one has asked for help or shown any difficulty. If she acts on the plan, an assumption about age does the work that a simple question should do. At work, age is a protected trait under the Minnesota Human Rights Act and, for people 40 and older, the federal Age Discrimination in Employment Act.

Sana can pause and name the purpose: a clear explanation of the next step. Then she can ask both colleagues the same question about that task. You can practice the same move privately. Name the assumption, name the fact you are missing and name the decision it could change.

inThisLesson: Tell a quick assumption apart from information about the person and the task.
Identify the age-to-technology assumption in the practice case.
Choose a next step that checks the assumption against the task.
Use the practice case or private reflection.
lessons.keyStatement: An assumption can be noticed and set aside before it decides anything.

flashcards.back: A quick connection the mind makes from past patterns. It saves time, but it can be wrong about the person in front of you.
Facts about this person and this task, rather than a general belief about a group.
A characteristic, such as age, race, color, national origin, sex, religion or disability, that civil rights law says cannot be the reason for worse treatment at work or in services.
Name the assumption, name the missing fact and ask a question about the task.

accordion.heading: Three moves when an assumption shows up

items.title: Name it
items.body: Sana can say to herself what came to mind without treating it as a fact about Dev. Naming it keeps the next step specific. It does not make her a bad colleague, and she does not need to share it.

items.title: Follow it to the decision
items.body: The assumption shows up in two places: who goes first and who is offered help. Looking at those two choices is more useful than debating whether Sana meant well. Dev may want help, or may not. The way to learn is to ask.

items.title: Return to the task
items.body: The team needs a clear explanation of the page’s next step. Age tells Sana nothing about that. A task question gathers the information she actually needs. It also avoids replacing one group assumption with its opposite.

tabs.label: Act on the assumption
tabs.body: Sana picks Quinn because it feels right. She has no evidence that Quinn explains the step more clearly, or that Dev needs help. The comfortable choice steers attention away from what the task requires.

tabs.label: Turn it into a label
tabs.body: Emmett tells Sana she is prejudiced because of one passing thought. That goes beyond what anyone knows. It also makes people less willing to look at their own decisions. The useful question is still what the thought could change and what would check it.

tabs.label: Notice and check
tabs.body: Sana names the assumption and asks both colleagues the same task question. This does not promise that the thought will never return. It does keep the decision tied to information about the task.

check.question: Which statement best describes the opening case?
check.correct: Sana noticed an age-to-technology assumption, and it tells her nothing yet about either colleague’s skill.
wrong: Quinn’s age shows that Quinn will explain the page better.
Dev’s age shows that Dev needs basic help.
One passing thought shows that Sana cannot be trusted with decisions.
check.feedbackCorrect: The assumption is real, but it is not information about Dev or Quinn. The next step is a task question for both of them.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Age does not show how well someone explains a page or whether they need help. One passing thought is also not a verdict on Sana. Look at the decision the thought could change and the fact that would check it.

sorting.heading: Sort what Sana knows from what she assumed

items.text: Dev and Quinn offered to walk the team through the page.
Dev is older than Quinn.
How would each of you explain the page’s next step?
Is there any part of the page you would like help with?
Quinn will explain the page better because Quinn is younger.
Sana’s passing thought shows she is prejudiced.

lessons.next: Next, see how the same criteria and a second reader keep assumptions out of choices about people.

scenario.context: Practice case: Sana has the age-to-technology thought before she knows how either colleague uses the page.
options: Name the assumption to herself and ask both colleagues the same question about the page’s next step.
Ask Quinn to go first because the choice feels natural.
Offer Dev basic help in advance so the session goes smoothly.
responses: This keeps the choice tied to the task. Both colleagues get the same chance to show what they know.
A feeling of fit is not information about the task. This choice lets age decide who goes first.
The help may be kindly meant, but no one asked for it. Offering it only to Dev treats age as a sign of need.

lessons.transfer: Think of a recent decision at work, or use Sana’s case. Privately name one assumption, one fact that was missing and one question that would have checked it.

move.control: You decide what question to ask before you act on a first impression.
move.failure: A familiar assumption decides who goes first, who gets help or who gets the opportunity.
move.next: Before your next assignment or invitation, write the task question you will ask everyone, and ask it of each person.

lessons.title: Use the same criteria for everyone, and add a second reader
lessons.summary: Written criteria applied to every person, with a second reader who scores separately, make it harder for a shortcut in judgment to decide who gets an opportunity.
lessons.objective: Apply written criteria and an independent second reader to a choice about people.
objectives: Apply written criteria and an independent second reader to a choice about people.
Explain what three studies found when only a name, or what reviewers could see, changed.
Set criteria before reviewing any names or materials.
takeaways: Write the criteria before you look at anyone’s materials.
Apply the same criteria, in the same way, to every person.
A second reader who scores separately catches what one reader misses.
lessons.statement: Decide what counts before you know whose work you are reading.

image.caption: Four people stand together in a hallway holding documents and a laptop.

intro.heading: Why criteria come first
intro.body:
Sana’s team is choosing two staff members for a six-month project assignment that builds new skills. Eight people have applied with short written statements. The supervisor, Ana, asks Sana and Emmett to help review them.

Studies of real choices show why the process matters. A 2004 field experiment in the American Economic Review sent about 5,000 fictional resumes to job ads in Boston and Chicago. The resumes were matched in quality. Those with names more common among white Americans received about 50 percent more callbacks than the same resumes with names more common among Black Americans.

A 2012 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences asked university science faculty to rate an application for a lab manager job. The application was identical except for the name, John or Jennifer. Faculty rated the John version as more competent and offered a higher starting salary. A study published in 2000 found that when orchestras auditioned musicians behind a screen, women became more likely to advance.

In each study, qualifications did not change. Only the name, or what the reviewer could see, changed. The point is not that reviewers meant harm. It is that a choice made without set criteria leaves room for shortcuts.

So Ana sets the process before anyone reads a statement. The team writes three criteria tied to the assignment: experience with the work, a clear plan for what the person would learn and availability for the full six months. Each reviewer rates every statement against the same criteria and writes a one-line reason. Sana and Emmett score separately before they compare. Where their ratings differ, they go back to the statement and the criteria, not to their impressions of the person.

The U.S. Office of Personnel Management describes the same idea for interviews: the same job-related questions, asked in the same order and rated on the same scale. It also matches civil rights law. Under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act and the Minnesota Human Rights Act, choices about assignments and training cannot turn on race, sex, age or another protected trait. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s March 2025 technical assistance, “What You Should Know About DEI-Related Discrimination at Work,” applies that rule to training, mentoring and selection for opportunities.

inThisLesson: Apply written criteria and an independent second reader to a choice about people.
Explain what three studies found when only a name, or what reviewers could see, changed.
Set criteria before reviewing any names or materials.
Use the practice case or private reflection.
lessons.keyStatement: Set the criteria first, apply them to everyone and let two readers score separately.

flashcards.back: A short written list of job-related standards, set before review and applied to every person in the same way.
A second person who rates the same materials separately, before any discussion, so one first impression does not set the result.
One or two sentences linking a rating to the criteria. It lets someone else see how the decision was made.
Connected to what the work actually requires, rather than to style, background or familiarity.

accordion.heading: Three parts of a fair review

items.title: Set criteria before you read
items.body: When criteria come after the review, they tend to describe the person the reviewer already liked. Writing them first, from the assignment’s real demands, keeps them tied to the work.

items.title: Score separately, then compare
items.body: If Emmett hears Sana’s view first, he may lean toward it. Separate scoring keeps two independent reads. A difference between them is a prompt to look again at the evidence.

items.title: Write the reason down
items.body: A short written reason makes the choice explainable to the applicant, the supervisor and anyone who reviews it later. It also shows quickly when a rating rests on something outside the criteria.

tabs.heading: Three ways to run the review

tabs.label: Gut feel
tabs.body: Each reviewer picks the statements that feel strongest. The choices may be good, but no one can explain them. Familiar styles get an easier route.

tabs.label: Criteria after the fact
tabs.body: The team picks its favorites, then writes criteria that fit them. This looks structured, but it carries the same shortcut forward.

tabs.label: Criteria first, two readers
tabs.body: The team sets criteria, scores separately, writes reasons and compares. It takes a little longer. Every applicant meets the same standard, and the team has a record.

check.question: In the 2004 resume study, what differed between the resumes that got more callbacks and those that got fewer?
check.correct: Only the name at the top; the qualifications were matched.
wrong: The city where each resume was sent.
check.feedbackCorrect: The study held qualifications steady and changed only the name. That is why it points to the decision process rather than the applicants.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The study matched qualifications and sent resumes to ads in both cities. Only the name changed, so the gap in callbacks came from how readers responded to the name.

items.text: Write three job-related criteria before reading any statement.
Each reviewer scores separately and writes a reason.
Pick the statement that sounds most like how my team talks.
Decide the criteria after choosing the favorites.
Hold one of the two spots for applicants of a particular race.
Prefer the younger applicant because the assignment uses new software.

lessons.next: Next, replace a presumed skill with a question every person can answer.

scenario.context: Practice case: Sana and Emmett finish scoring separately. Sana rated one statement a 2 on “clear learning plan.” Emmett rated it a 4.
options: Average the two numbers and move on.
Return to the statement and the written criterion, read each other’s reasons and agree on a rating they can explain.
Use Sana’s rating because she knows the applicant better.
responses: Averaging hides the disagreement. It skips the moment when a second reader is most useful.
The difference is a signal to look again at the evidence. The agreed rating and its reason become part of the record.
Knowing an applicant is information outside the criteria. It can favor people the reviewer already knows.

lessons.transfer: Pick a choice your team makes about people, such as assignments, training spots or who presents, or use the six-month assignment case. Privately list the criteria you would set first.

move.control: You can set criteria and ask for a second reader on decisions you help make.
move.failure: Criteria are written after the choice, or one reader’s first impression decides the result.
move.next: For the next selection you help with, write the criteria before anyone reviews materials, and ask a colleague to score separately.

lessons.title: Replace a presumed skill with a relevant question
lessons.summary: When Sana asks Dev and Quinn the same task question, the answers show something age could not: what each person actually knows about the page.
lessons.objective: Ask a task question that gathers real information instead of relying on a presumed skill.
objectives: Ask a task question that gathers real information instead of relying on a presumed skill.
Describe what Dev’s and Quinn’s answers add to the page review.
Avoid replacing one group assumption with its opposite.
takeaways: The same question for everyone gives information you can compare.
The answer can surprise you; let it change the plan.
Do not trade one group assumption for its reverse.
lessons.statement: Ask the question the task needs, and ask it of everyone.

image.caption: Four people stand together in a hallway holding documents and a laptop.

intro.heading: What the question shows
intro.body:
Sana sets aside her first thought. She asks Dev and Quinn the same question: “How would you explain what happens when someone uses the page’s next step?”

Dev walks through the question list step by step and points out a label that could confuse readers. Quinn asks a question instead: does sending a question through the page start a service application? The draft does not say. That gap matters to the people who will use the page.

Neither answer matches what Sana expected. Dev knows the steps well. Quinn found a real problem in the draft. If Sana had acted on her first thought, she would have missed both.

There is a second trap. Sana should not now conclude that older colleagues are better with pages, or that younger colleagues ask more questions. That only reverses the shortcut. What she learned is about Dev, Quinn and this page.

Asking the same question does not mean everyone must answer in the same way. People can show what they know by explaining, demonstrating or asking. If someone needs an accommodation to take part, it goes through the usual process with the person or area responsible. What stays the same is the question and the standard.

inThisLesson: Ask a task question that gathers real information instead of relying on a presumed skill.
Describe what Dev’s and Quinn’s answers add to the page review.
Avoid replacing one group assumption with its opposite.
Use the practice case or private reflection.
lessons.keyStatement: A good question replaces a guess with information about the person and the task.

flashcards.back: A question about what the work requires, asked of each person in the same way.
Swapping one group belief for its opposite, such as “older people are better at this.” It is still a shortcut.
Everyone is held to the same criteria. How they show what they know can vary, including through an accommodation.
Quinn’s question shows that the page does not say whether a question starts an application. That is useful information for the team.

items.title: Let the answer replace the guess
items.body: Dev’s step-by-step account is direct information. It replaces the guess about age and comfort with technology.

items.title: Treat a question as a contribution
items.body: Quinn’s question found a gap that readers would have hit. A question is not a sign of weak skill. Here it improved the page.

items.title: Do not build a new rule
items.body: One answer from Dev and one from Quinn says nothing about their age groups. Keep the lesson tied to the people and the task.

tabs.heading: Three ways to use the answers

tabs.label: Keep the first plan
tabs.body: Sana thanks both colleagues and still asks Quinn to lead. The answers did not change anything, so the question was only for show.

tabs.label: Flip the assumption
tabs.body: Sana decides that older staff are better with pages. The shortcut has changed direction, but it is still a shortcut.

tabs.label: Use what was learned
tabs.body: Sana asks Dev to walk the team through the steps and takes Quinn’s question to the person responsible for the page. Each choice rests on what the person said.

check.question: What is the main thing Sana learned from asking the same question?
check.correct: What Dev and Quinn each know about this page, which her first thought could not tell her.
wrong: That older staff are better with technology than she thought.
That Quinn is less skilled because Quinn asked a question.
That task questions are only useful in hiring.
check.feedbackCorrect: The answers are information about two people and one task. They do not support a new rule about any age group.
check.feedbackIncorrect: One answer from each person does not describe an age group, and asking a question is not a weakness. Task questions help in any choice about people, from presenting to assignments.

items.text: Dev can explain the question-list steps.
The draft does not say whether a question starts an application.
How readers outside the team will understand the page.
Whether Dev or Quinn wants to lead the session.
Older staff are better at explaining pages.
People who ask questions understand less.

lessons.next: Next, learn what a response style means before judging it.

scenario.context: Practice case: after hearing both answers, Emmett says, “Interesting. I guess we had it backwards about age.”
scenario.prompt: What is the most useful reply?
options: “Maybe. Let’s have the older staff lead from now on.”
“Let’s just go back to picking whoever volunteers first.”
“I would not draw a rule about age either way. Let’s use what Dev and Quinn told us about this page.”
responses: This turns the assumption around but keeps it. Age is still deciding.
Volunteer order can work for a small task, but it ignores the information the team just gathered.
This keeps the lesson tied to the people and the task, and it avoids a new group rule.

lessons.transfer: Privately write a task question you could ask everyone before a choice in your work, or write one for the page review in the case.

move.control: You choose the question, and you choose to let the answer change the plan.
move.failure: The question is asked, but the first assumption, or its reverse, still decides.
move.next: The next time you invite someone to present, review or lead, ask each person the same task question first.

lessons.title: Learn what a response means before judging it
lessons.summary: A quiet listener and a fast paraphraser can both be engaged. Asking what a response means keeps a difference in style from becoming a judgment.
lessons.objective: Ask about the meaning of a response style before drawing a conclusion from it.
objectives: Ask about the meaning of a response style before drawing a conclusion from it.
Identify the two quick readings Sana makes in the practice session.
Offer more than one way for people to take part.
takeaways: Quiet does not always mean uninterested.
A fast summary does not always mean full understanding.
Offering more than one way to respond helps everyone take part.
lessons.statement: Before you read meaning into a response, ask about it.

image.caption: Four people stand together in a hallway holding documents and a laptop.

intro.heading: Two quick readings
intro.body:
Later, Sana leads a practice session on the revised page with two other colleagues, Rhea and Len. Rhea listens without speaking for most of the session and takes notes. Len restates each step in his own words almost as soon as Sana finishes it.

Sana’s quick readings are that Rhea is not interested and that Len already understands. Both are shortcuts. She has not asked either of them.

At the end, Sana asks each person how the session worked for them. Rhea says she likes to hear the full sequence before speaking, so she does not ask something the next step answers. Her notes include two careful edits. Len says restating is how he checks his own understanding, and he asks Sana to correct him when he is off. One of his restatements was, in fact, slightly wrong.

Communication habits differ by person, family, work history, language and culture. The Council of Europe’s guidance on intercultural competence describes asking about meaning instead of applying your own default. That does not mean assigning a style to a group. Rhea and Len each explained their own habit.

Sana can now offer more than one way to take part: a pause for questions after the full sequence, and a chance to restate and be corrected. Both options are open to everyone. Neither is tied to who a person is.

inThisLesson: Ask about the meaning of a response style before drawing a conclusion from it.
Identify the two quick readings Sana makes in the practice session.
Offer more than one way for people to take part.
Use the practice case or private reflection.
lessons.keyStatement: A response style belongs to a person; ask the person what it means.

flashcards.back: The way a person shows attention or understanding, such as listening quietly, asking questions or restating.
The style a group treats as normal without noticing, such as speaking up quickly. It can become the rule everyone is measured against.
A short, open question such as “How did that format work for you?” in place of a guess.
Several ways to take part, offered to everyone, so no one has to match one style.

accordion.heading: Check the reading before the judgment

items.title: Quiet is information, not a verdict
items.body: Rhea’s silence could mean many things. Her notes and her answer show careful attention. Without asking, Sana would have recorded the opposite.

items.title: Speed is not the same as accuracy
items.body: Len’s fast restating looked like full understanding. One restatement was off. His habit is useful because it invites correction.

items.title: Do not turn a person into a group
items.body: Sana learns about Rhea and Len, not about any culture or generation. Asking each person keeps it that way.

tabs.heading: Three ways to run the next session

tabs.label: Reward the fastest voice
tabs.body: Sana calls on whoever responds first. Quick speakers shape the result, and careful listeners’ edits get lost.

tabs.label: Assign styles by group
tabs.body: Sana decides that people from certain backgrounds prefer quiet. That is a new assumption, and it may be wrong about the person in front of her.

tabs.label: Offer options to everyone
tabs.body: Sana builds in a pause after the full sequence and invites restatements. Everyone can use either one.

check.question: Which conclusion fits what Sana learned?
check.correct: Rhea and Len were both engaged in different ways, and asking showed what each style meant.
wrong: Rhea was not interested because she was quiet.
Len understood everything because he restated each step.
Quiet listeners usually come from particular cultures.
check.feedbackCorrect: Asking turned two guesses into information. The options Sana offers next are open to everyone.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Silence and speed did not mean what Sana first assumed. A style belongs to a person, not a group, so asking each person is the reliable check.

items.text: Rhea took notes and spoke little.
Len restated steps quickly.
Rhea likes to hear the full sequence before speaking.
Len restates to check his own understanding.
Rhea was not interested.
Len understood every step.

lessons.next: Next, see when a concern is no longer a learning moment but a civil rights duty.

scenario.context: Practice case: in the next session, a new participant, Tomas, says very little.
options: Note that Tomas seems disengaged and move on.
At a natural break, ask the whole group how the format is working, and offer the pause and the restating options to everyone.
Ask Tomas in front of the group why he is so quiet.
responses: That repeats the first quick reading without checking it.
This checks meaning without singling anyone out, and it gives everyone the same options.
Singling out one person can feel like pressure, and it may not get an honest answer.

lessons.transfer: Privately think of a response style you tend to read quickly, or use Rhea’s and Len’s case. Write the question that would check your reading.

move.control: You can ask about meaning and offer more than one way to take part.
move.failure: One response style becomes the standard, and other styles are judged against it.
move.next: In your next meeting or session, offer two ways to respond and ask the group how the format worked.

lessons.title: Know when a concern is a civil rights duty
lessons.summary: Checking your own assumptions is personal learning. A discrimination allegation is different: managers report it right away, and the person or area responsible handles it.
lessons.objective: Recognize when a concern must go to the person or area responsible rather than stay a learning conversation.
objectives: Recognize when a concern must go to the person or area responsible rather than stay a learning conversation.
Describe a manager’s reporting duty under Minnesota Management and Budget Policy 1436.
Name the civil rights laws that apply to employment and to services.
takeaways: Reflection is personal; reporting duties are required.
A report is not a finding; it starts a fair process.
Retaliation for raising a concern is prohibited.
lessons.statement: Learning about assumptions never replaces a duty to report.

image.caption: Four people stand together in a hallway holding documents and a laptop.

intro.heading: When the concern is about a decision
intro.body:
In a separate practice case, a staff member, Pat, tells manager Oren that a team lead keeps giving new-system assignments to younger staff. Pat says the team lead has said older staff “won’t pick it up.”

This is no longer a lesson about checking one’s own thoughts. It is an allegation that a protected trait, age, is affecting job assignments. Minnesota Management and Budget Policy 1436, Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited, requires managers and supervisors to report allegations like this right away. They report to human resources or the agency’s Affirmative Action Officer and then follow the complaint and investigation procedures.

Oren does not need proof, an apology, a training course or a talk with the team lead before he reports. A report is not a finding. The person or area responsible looks into the facts. Raising a concern is protected, and retaliation against Pat or anyone who takes part is prohibited under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act and the Minnesota Human Rights Act.

The same idea applies to services. Title VI of the Civil Rights Act bars discrimination by race, color or national origin in programs that receive federal funds, and it requires meaningful access for people with limited English. The Americans with Disabilities Act and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act require equal access for people with disabilities. The Minnesota Human Rights Act covers both employment and public services. Concerns from members of the public go to the person or area responsible for civil rights complaints at DHS.

The DHS Equity Policy sets daily responsibilities and the tools for formal equity analysis. Reflection in this course does not complete that work. Native American and Tribal-specific matters go to DHS Tribal and Urban Indian Relations and the person or area responsible.

inThisLesson: Recognize when a concern must go to the person or area responsible rather than stay a learning conversation.
Describe a manager’s reporting duty under Minnesota Management and Budget Policy 1436.
Name the civil rights laws that apply to employment and to services.
Use the practice case or private reflection.
lessons.keyStatement: When a protected trait may have affected a decision, the report comes first.

flashcards.back: A manager or supervisor who learns of a harassment or discrimination allegation based on a protected trait reports it right away to human resources or the Affirmative Action Officer.
A report starts a fair process to learn the facts. It does not decide that anything happened.
Treating someone worse because they raised a concern or took part in an investigation. It is prohibited.
The part of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 that bars discrimination by race, color or national origin in programs that receive federal funds.

items.title: Learning track
items.body: Noticing your own assumptions, setting criteria and asking task questions are habits you choose. They are private.

items.title: Duty track
items.body: An allegation that a protected trait affected a decision goes to the person or area responsible right away. A learning conversation does not delay it.

items.title: Both can happen
items.body: After reporting, Oren can still use fair process in his own decisions, such as written criteria for assignments and a second reader. That supports the duty; it does not replace it.

tabs.label: Handle it informally first
tabs.body: Oren plans to talk with the team lead and see if things improve. That delays a required report and leaves Pat without the protected process.

tabs.label: Ask for proof first
tabs.body: Oren asks Pat to bring evidence before he acts. The policy does not require proof before reporting. Finding the facts is the investigation’s job.

tabs.label: Report and support
tabs.body: Oren reports to human resources right away, tells Pat what happens next and watches for any sign of retaliation. He does not decide the outcome himself.

check.question: What does Oren need before he reports Pat’s concern?
check.correct: Nothing more; the allegation itself is enough to report.
wrong: A conversation with the team lead to hear the other side.
Completion of a course on checking assumptions.
check.feedbackCorrect: The policy asks managers to report right away. Gathering facts and hearing from everyone is the job of the investigation that follows.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Proof, a side conversation or a course would each delay a required report. The person or area responsible gathers the facts after the report.

items.text: Reflect privately on an assumption you noticed.
Practice writing criteria for a sample assignment.
Report a discrimination allegation to human resources right away.
Provide language access for a member of the public with limited English.
Wait for proof before reporting an allegation.
Move Pat off the team after the complaint.

lessons.next: Next, write down the reason, check the results and plan when to look again.

scenario.context: Practice case: Oren reports Pat’s concern. A week later, the team lead asks Oren to move Pat to another team, saying the mood has been tense.
options: Approve the move to calm the team.
Ask Pat whether Pat would rather leave.
Decline the move, tell the person handling the investigation about the request and keep Pat’s assignments on the same criteria as before.
responses: Moving Pat after the complaint could be retaliation, whatever the intent.
The question may sound kind, but it puts pressure on Pat and could still lead to a retaliatory result.
This prevents a change that could be retaliation and keeps decisions tied to the usual criteria.

lessons.transfer: Privately note where the reporting route is in your area, or use Oren’s case to list the steps he takes.

move.control: You can learn the reporting route and keep your own decisions on written criteria.
move.failure: A learning conversation, a request for proof or an informal fix delays a required report.

lessons.title: Write the reason, check the result and look again
lessons.summary: A fair decision leaves a record, and a fair process gets checked. Write down the reason, look at who received opportunities over time and set a date to revisit.
lessons.objective: Record the reason for a decision and plan a simple check of its results.
objectives: Record the reason for a decision and plan a simple check of its results.
Describe what Sana’s team will review after three months.
State honestly what has changed and what has not.
takeaways: A written reason makes a decision explainable.
Looking at results over time shows patterns one decision cannot.
Checking your process is ongoing; no course makes assumptions disappear.
lessons.statement: Write down why, look at what happened and set a date to look again.

image.caption: Four people stand together in a hallway holding documents and a laptop.

intro.heading: Closing the loop
intro.body:
Back on Sana’s team, the page review is done and the two project spots are filled. Sana writes a short note for each choice: who was invited to present the page and why, and how the criteria applied to each assignment. Each reason points to the task or the criteria, not to a sense of fit.

Ana, the supervisor, adds a check. In three months, the team will look at who has been invited to present, review or lead, and who received development assignments. If a pattern appears, such as the same few people always chosen, the team will look at its criteria and its invitation process. The check looks at the process; it does not single out any person.

This follows the DHS Equity Policy and Equity Analysis Toolkit, which ask teams to consider who a decision affects and how its results will be measured. A process that looks neutral can still produce unequal results. The way to know is to look.

Sana can also be honest about what changed. She now notices one kind of assumption more often, and she has a question she asks everyone. That is a real gain. It is not proof that her assumptions are gone, and it is not a measure of better services. That is why the team relies on process, not good intentions alone.

You can do the same in your own role. Pick one recurring choice about people, write the reason each time and set a date to look at the results.

lessons.keyStatement: A written reason and a planned check turn a good intention into a fair process.

flashcards.back: A short record of a choice and the criteria or task fact it rests on.
A planned look at who received an opportunity over time, to see whether the process works as intended.
A set time to review criteria and results, so the check actually happens.
A clear statement of what changed, such as a new question you ask, without claiming more than you know.

accordion.heading: Three parts of closing the loop

items.title: Write the reason
items.body: A one- or two-line reason tied to the criteria lets others understand and question the choice. It also helps you see when a reason drifts toward fit or familiarity.

items.title: Look at the pattern
items.body: One choice rarely shows a problem. Many choices over months can. A short review of who got which opportunities makes patterns visible.

items.title: Adjust the process, not the person
items.body: If a pattern appears, the fix is in the criteria, the invitation route or who reviews. It is never a preference for or against any group.

tabs.label: Declare success
tabs.body: The team decides the course worked and moves on. No one checks results, and old habits can return unnoticed.

tabs.label: Pick people to match a target
tabs.body: The team plans to choose people to reach a set ratio by race or another protected trait. That is treating people differently because of a protected trait, which the law does not allow.

tabs.label: Record, review and revisit
tabs.body: The team writes reasons, reviews who got opportunities in three months and adjusts the process if needed.

check.question: What should the three-month review focus on?
check.correct: Whether the criteria and invitation process give everyone a fair chance at opportunities.
wrong: Setting a quota for the next round of assignments.
Proving the course removed everyone’s assumptions.
check.feedbackCorrect: The review looks at the process and its results. Any fix goes into the criteria and routes, open to everyone.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The review is not about labeling people or setting quotas, and no course can prove assumptions are gone. It looks at whether the process works fairly and what to adjust.

items.text: Each choice has a written reason tied to the criteria.
Sana asks every presenter the same task question.
Whether the same few people keep getting chosen.
Whether the criteria fit the assignments well.
The team no longer makes assumptions.
Services improved because of this course.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to plan one decision note and one results check in your own role.

scenario.context: Practice case: at the three-month review, the team sees that the same two people have presented at every meeting.
scenario.prompt: What is a useful next step?
options: Look at how presenters are invited, and add a step where everyone is asked the same task question in turn.
Bar the two people from presenting for six months.
Decide nothing is wrong because no one has complained.
responses: This fixes the route without penalizing anyone, and it keeps the opportunity open to all.
Penalizing two people does not fix the invitation process, and it treats them unfairly.
Complaints are not the only signal. The pattern itself is a reason to look at the process.

lessons.transfer: Privately choose one recurring decision in your role, or use the presenter case. Write the reason you would record and the date you would look again.

move.control: You can write reasons for your own choices and plan when to check results.
move.failure: A choice is made once and never checked, so a pattern grows unnoticed.
move.next: Choose one recurring decision in your role, record the reason each time for the next month and set a date to review who received the opportunity.

jobAid.subtitle: Notice the assumption, use the same criteria, ask the task question, keep duties separate and check the results.
remember: An assumption, a task answer and a decision each need their own evidence.
Use a practice case or private reflection. No personal record, score or disclosure is needed.

sections.heading: Notice the assumption
items: Name what came to mind, the fact you are missing and the decision it could change.
Treat a familiar feeling as a prompt to check, not as evidence.

sections.heading: Set criteria first
items: Write job-related criteria before anyone reviews names or materials, and apply them to every person.
Have a second reader score separately. Write a reason for each rating, then compare and resolve differences against the criteria.

sections.heading: Ask the task question
items: Ask everyone the same question the task needs, and let the answer change the plan.
Do not replace one group assumption with its reverse. Handle accommodation requests through the usual process.

sections.heading: Ask about meaning
items: Before judging a response style, ask how the format worked.
Offer more than one way to take part, open to everyone.

sections.heading: Keep duties separate
items: Managers and supervisors report harassment or discrimination allegations right away to human resources or the Affirmative Action Officer under Minnesota Management and Budget Policy 1436. No proof, apology or course comes first.
Retaliation is prohibited. Title VI, the Americans with Disabilities Act, Section 504 and the Minnesota Human Rights Act apply to services; concerns go to the person or area responsible.
The DHS Equity Policy and Equity Analysis Toolkit keep their own steps. Native American and Tribal-specific matters go to DHS Tribal and Urban Indian Relations and the person or area responsible.

sections.heading: Close the loop
items: Write a short reason for each choice about people.
Set a date to review who received opportunities. Adjust criteria or routes, never by preferring or excluding any group.

sources.title: Bertrand and Mullainathan (2004) — Are Emily and Greg More Employable than Lakisha and Jamal? American Economic Review
sources.note: Field experiment sending matched resumes to job ads in Boston and Chicago; names more common among white Americans received about 50 percent more callbacks. Used in lesson 2.

sources.title: Moss-Racusin and others (2012) — Science faculty’s subtle gender biases favor male students, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.note: Faculty rated an identical lab manager application as more competent and offered a higher salary when it carried a male name. Used in lesson 2.

sources.title: Goldin and Rouse (2000) — Orchestrating Impartiality: The Impact of “Blind” Auditions on Female Musicians, American Economic Review
sources.note: Found that auditioning behind a screen made it more likely that women advanced in orchestra auditions. Used in lesson 2.

sources.title: U.S. Office of Personnel Management — Structured Interviews
sources.note: Federal guidance on asking the same job-related questions of every candidate and rating answers on a set scale.

sources.title: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (2025) — What You Should Know About DEI-Related Discrimination at Work
sources.note: Technical assistance explaining that employment actions based on race, sex or another protected trait, including in training, mentoring and selection for opportunities, are unlawful whatever the stated goal.

sources.title: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission — Age Discrimination
sources.note: Explains the federal Age Discrimination in Employment Act, which protects applicants and employees 40 and older in assignments, training and other terms of employment.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes chapter 363A — Minnesota Human Rights Act
sources.note: State law prohibiting discrimination in employment, public services and other areas, including based on age, and reprisal for raising a concern.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget Policy 1436: Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited
sources.note: Requires managers and supervisors to report harassment or discrimination allegations based on a protected trait right away to human resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and to follow the complaint procedures. A course, apology or request for proof cannot delay that report.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division — Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
sources.note: Prohibits discrimination based on race, color or national origin in federally funded programs, including meaningful access for people with limited English.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Sets daily responsibilities and the tools and roles for formal equity analysis. Reflection in this course does not complete that work.

sources.title: Council of Europe: Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Describes learning to ask about meaning in communication rather than applying one’s own default. Used in lesson 4, where each person explains their own habit.

sources.title: DHS: Content and writing guidelines
sources.note: Supports plain, accurate written reasons and clear task questions, like the decision notes in lesson 6.
